title: "The 2PL Is a Tiny Neural Network: Width, Depth, and Held-Out Prediction on 242 Item Response Tables"
description: |
  The Rasch and 2PL models are two-embedding networks with no hidden layer.
  Part I builds them in PyTorch and checks them against `mirt`. Part II widens
  and deepens them and asks, on 24 IRW tables scored with the InterModel
  Vigorish, whether a neural network predicts held-out item responses any
  better than the 2PL. Mostly it does not: where a network wins, the win is a
  second dimension, and an ordinary two-dimensional MIRT finds it as well as a
  multilayer perceptron does. Part III applies a selection rule to the whole
  warehouse and fits both models on 242 tables: the median table gains nothing
  and the mean gain matches the published benchmark, carried by the seventh of
  the corpus whose tables mix items running in opposite directions. Part IV
  takes apart a small gap between the torch 2PL and the `mirt` 2PL: the
  estimator explains it, and fixing the scale of the person parameters does
  not.

#| label: setup

# Part I. The 2PL as a neural network {#part-i}

## Motivation

A logistic item response model is a very small neural network. The Rasch
model takes a person, looks up one number for them ($\theta_p$), takes an
item, looks up one number for it ($d_i$, the negative of the difficulty),
adds the two, and passes the sum through a sigmoid. In PyTorch terms that is
two `nn.Embedding` layers and no hidden layer at all. The 2PL adds a second
item lookup, the slope $a_i$, and multiplies before it adds. Once the models
are written this way, a question that is awkward to pose in the psychometric
idiom becomes the obvious next step: what happens when the network is made
wider or deeper? Does a neural network predict item responses better than the
2PL? Both words are defined precisely below, but in short: width is how many
numbers the network looks up for each person and item, and depth is how many
layers sit between those numbers and the predicted response.

The question is not new. Variational IRT [@wu2020variational] and the
recommender-systems literature [@koren2009matrix; @he2017ncf] both treat
person-by-item data as a matrix to be factorised and have explored exactly
these widenings. What is missing is a comparison on an honest footing: the
same held-out cells, the same prior on persons, the same scoring rule, across
enough real tables of different kinds to see where a wider network helps and
where it does not. That is the contribution here. We build the classical
models in PyTorch, confirm that they recover what `mirt` [@chalmers2012mirt]
recovers, widen and deepen them, and score every model on held-out responses
from 24 IRW tables with the InterModel Vigorish [IMV, @domingue2024imv],
which puts every gain on the scale of a bet. Two flexible one-dimensional
models from `mirt`, the monotonic polynomial [@falk2016monotonic] and the
logistic positive exponent [@samejima2000lpe], join the comparison, because
they make the opposite move from the networks: they change the *shape* of
the item curve while keeping a single dimension.

The short version of the answer is that on a test built to measure one thing,
nothing beats the 2PL; where a network wins, the win is a second dimension, and
a two-dimensional MIRT finds it as well as a deeper network does. We then put
that result to a harder test, applying a selection rule to the whole warehouse
rather than a judgment to 24 tables, and fitting the 2PL against a
two-dimensional MIRT on all 242 tables that qualify. The median table gains
nothing; the mean gain, +0.0025, matches the published benchmark and is carried
almost entirely by a seventh of the corpus. Those tables have something in
common: each mixes items that run in opposite directions, which the 2PL fits by
giving some of them a negative slope. All of
this holds at the sizes we fit here: tables are capped at 5,000 respondents and
116 items, and scale is the one advantage a wider network is supposed to have,
so the null is a null at this scale.

The page is in four parts. [Part I](#part-i) builds the
models and checks them against `mirt`. [Part II](#part-ii) widens and deepens
them on the 24 tables. [Part III](#part-iii) asks how often the one move that
worked actually works, across 242 tables chosen by rule, and closes by asking
what the tables that gain have in common. One of the comparisons also turned up
a small but consistent gap between the same 2PL fit in torch and in `mirt`;
[Part IV](#part-iv) takes it apart.

## Data and methods

### Dataset selection

We wanted tables that would spread across the kinds of structure a wider
network might find, rather than a random sample of the warehouse. The 24
tables fall into five groups, fixed in `nn_irt_helpers.py`:

- **Achievement and ability tests** built to measure one thing (a Brazilian
  medical residency exam, an ENCCEJA Portuguese form, a Dutch listening test,
  a general intelligence measure, two vocabulary and ability samples).
- **Knowledge tests with heterogeneous content** (two COVID-19 knowledge
  scales, a financial literacy test, the Author Recognition Test), where the
  items range over topics and a single dimension is a convenience rather than
  a design.
- **Tests with a documented multidimensional structure** (the ECPE grammar
  test with its three-attribute Q-matrix, a mental-rotation test, a medical
  licensing exam).
- **Personality and clinical inventories** that mix several syndromes or
  facets in one table (the Woodworth Psychoneurotic Inventory, the NPI, the
  Taylor Manifest Anxiety scale, the Eysenck EPI, the MCMI, and four more).
- **Developmental screeners** (the ASQ and Denver items from the D-score
  project), which span motor, language and social domains and are
  age-adaptive, so each child answers only a slice of the items.

All are dense and dichotomous. The response values are checked at fetch time
rather than trusted from metadata; one candidate, `vocabulary_iq`, turned out
to be polytomous despite its metadata and was dropped (and the metadata
corrected upstream); two further candidates, `encceja_2025_em_cn` and
`mgkt_options`, were dropped because their full exports fail to load, so the
final 24 is a design choice filtered by what we could read. Tables with more
than 5,000 respondents or 116 items are subsampled to those caps with a fixed
seed, so that every fit on the page stays small enough to run on a laptop. This
selection is deliberate and it is *not* a sample: these 24 tables were picked
to span kinds of structure, which makes them good for showing where gains come
from and bad for estimating how often gains occur. A rule-based sweep over the
whole warehouse, reported [below](#away-from-the-hand-picked-tables-the-median-table-gains-nothing),
supplies the second thing.

```{python}
#| label: data
#| code-summary: "Fetch, subsample and split the tables"
data = {t: prepare(t) for t in TABLES}
sizes = pd.DataFrame({SHORT[t]: {"group": GROUP_OF[t], "table": t,
                                 "persons": int(d.pid.max() + 1), "items": int(d.iid.max() + 1),
                                 "test cells": int(d.test.sum()),
                                 "mean resp": round(float(d.resp.mean()), 2)}
                      for t, d in data.items()}).T
sizes
```

`prepare` calls `irw.fetch`, caches the table, subsamples, assigns integer
indices, and draws the holdout mask with a fixed seed. Sizes are after
subsampling.

### Held-out cells, not held-out people

Every model here has a parameter per person. A model cannot predict a person
it has never seen, so the usual split by rows (train on some people, test on
others) is not available. We hold out **cells** instead: 20% of each
person's responses, chosen at random, are hidden during training and
predicted afterwards. Every person and every item stays in the training set.
The same mask is used by every model, including the `mirt` fits, which see
the held-out cells as missing. This is the cross-validation design of the
IMV paper, and it is the only one that makes sense when persons are
parameters.

### The models, written as networks

The four model classes below are the whole of the modelling code. Each takes
a batch of person indices and item indices and returns a logit.

| Model | Person lookup | Item lookup | Combine | Parameters | On the residency exam |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rasch | $\theta_p$ (1 number) | $d_i$ (1 number) | $\theta_p + d_i$ | $N + J$ | 3,339 |
| 2PL | $\theta_p$ (1) | $a_i, d_i$ (2) | $a_i\theta_p + d_i$ | $N + 2J$ | 3,455 |
| MIRT, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf a_i$ ($k$), $d_i$ | $\mathbf a_i \cdot \boldsymbol\theta_p + d_i$ | $kN + (k+1)J$ | 6,794 |
| Multilayer perceptron (MLP), $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf v_i$ ($k$) | $\mathrm{MLP}([\boldsymbol\theta_p, \mathbf v_i])$ | $kN + kJ + $ decoder | 6,775 (small), 11,223 (large) |

Here $N$ is the number of persons and $J$ the number of items, and the
residency exam column counts parameters for the first table on the page
(3,223 persons, 116 items, $k = 2$). The decoder of the small MLP has 97
weights and that of the large one 4,545, so even the large network is mostly
embeddings: the step from one dimension to two more than doubles the
parameter count, and depth adds comparatively little on top.

Two words carry the argument from here on, so it is worth pinning them down.
**Width** is the size of the embeddings: how many numbers the network looks up
for each person and for each item, written $k$ in the table above. Widening a
model is adding latent dimensions, so a wider 2PL is a multidimensional 2PL and
nothing more exotic than that; the Rasch model and the 2PL have width 1, and
every wider model on this page has width 2. **Depth** is the number of hidden
layers between the embeddings and the logit. The Rasch model, the 2PL and the
MIRT have none: the looked-up numbers are combined by a dot product and that
sum *is* the logit. The two MLPs have one and two hidden layers respectively.

Put differently, width governs what the model can represent about a person and
an item, and depth governs how freely what has been represented is allowed to
combine. A dot product says that a person's standing on each dimension pays off
additively and at a rate set by the item; depth lets that payoff bend. The 2PL
is the width-1, depth-0 corner of this space, and every other model here moves
away from it in one direction or the other --- which is what makes "is a bigger
network better?" a question with two separate answers rather than one.

The models are written in slope-intercept form, $a_i\theta_p + d_i$, as
`mirt` writes them, rather than the textbook $a_i(\theta_p - b_i)$. This is
not cosmetic. In the textbook form the gradient for $b_i$ is scaled by
$a_i$, so the difficulties of weak items barely move during training, and a
slope kept positive by an exponential cannot fit an item keyed against the
trait, which several of the inventories below contain. The slope here is
signed and unconstrained.

The MIRT model is the compensatory multidimensional 2PL [@reckase2009mirt]:
$k$-dimensional person and item embeddings combined by a dot product, which
is also a rank-$k$ factorisation of the logit matrix. With $k=1$ it is the
2PL; we use $k=2$. The multilayer perceptron, the plain feed-forward
neural network and the thing most people mean by "a neural net", concatenates
the two embeddings and passes them through one or more hidden layers of
rectified linear units before a final linear layer produces the logit. The
interaction between person and item is then no longer constrained to be a
dot product; this is the shape used in neural collaborative filtering
[@he2017ncf]. We fit two sizes, both on $k=2$ embeddings: a small one with a
single hidden layer of 16 units, and a large one with two hidden layers of
64, so that depth is the only thing that changes between them.

### Estimation

The PyTorch models are fit by minibatch gradient descent (Adam) on the mean
negative log-likelihood plus a $N(0,1)$ prior on $\theta_p$, which makes each
fit a maximum a posteriori estimate rather than joint maximum likelihood (the
section that follows builds this up line by line). The prior is the only thing
identifying the scale of $\theta$ on this page, and it is used that way
throughout: everything in the body of the page is the MAP fit. The obvious alternative is to
standardise $\theta$ to mean zero and SD one inside the model, which fixes the
scale exactly rather than softly; [Part IV](#part-iv) fits every
model both ways and reports what that costs, which is why the prior is what we
use here. Each model is trained for
up to 30 epochs and the epoch with the lowest held-out loss is reported. That
is early stopping with the held-out set doing double duty as a validation
set; a production comparison would carve out a third split, and we return to
what this choice costs in the results.

The `mirt` models are fit offline by marginal maximum likelihood
[@bock1981marginal] on the same training cells, in
`nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`, and each held-out cell is predicted by its
posterior-predictive probability: the item curve integrated over the
person's posterior on a quadrature grid. Three models are fit this way: the
2PL again, as the marginal-likelihood anchor for the PyTorch 2PL; the
monotonic polynomial model, whose item curve is a flexible monotone function
rather than a logistic; and the logistic positive exponent (LPE) model, whose
item curve is asymmetric.

### Scoring

Every model is scored on the same held-out cells by log-loss and by the IMV
against the PyTorch 2PL. The IMV converts a log-loss improvement into a bet:
if model 0 predicts held-out responses as well as a coin with bias $w_0$ and
model 1 as well as a coin with bias $w_1$, the IMV is $(w_1 - w_0)/w_0$, the
relative gain in the bettor's edge. The [IMV vignette](imv.qmd) has the
derivation and the R package. In Python we use the
[`imvpy`](https://github.com/intermodelvigorish/imvpy) package, whose
`vanilla_imv` takes the baseline probabilities, the enhanced probabilities
and the outcomes, in that order. The definition is short enough to write
out, and the helper module does so; the two agree on the first table's
held-out cells to the fourth decimal, the residual being how extreme
probabilities are clipped.

```{python}
#| label: imv-check
#| code-fold: false
import inspect
print(inspect.getsource(imv))
_te = data["borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"]
_te = _te[_te.test]
_y, _p0 = _te.resp.values, np.full(len(_te), _te.resp.mean())
_p1 = np.clip(_p0 + 0.2 * (_y - 0.5), 0.05, 0.95)   # a deliberately better forecast
print(f"helper imv  {imv(_y, _p0, _p1):.5f}")
print(f"imvpy       {vanilla_imv(_p0, _p1, _y):.5f}")
```

## Building the network, step by step

Before the comparison, we write the 2PL as a network from nothing but
`torch`, on one table, so that each piece can be seen. The helper module used
later is this code with bookkeeping added.

### 1. Long data is already the right shape

A neural network consumes one training example at a time, and an item
response is one example: a person index, an item index, a 0/1 outcome.
Nothing has to be reshaped to a wide matrix; IRW's long format is the
network's native input. Three integer-coded columns become three tensors.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
d = data["borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"]
train = d[~d.test]
P = torch.tensor(train.pid.values)                        # person index, 0..n_persons-1
I = torch.tensor(train.iid.values)                        # item index,   0..n_items-1
Y = torch.tensor(train.resp.values, dtype=torch.float32)  # 0/1 response
n_p, n_i = int(d.pid.max() + 1), int(d.iid.max() + 1)
P[:5], I[:5], Y[:5], (n_p, n_i)
```

### 2. An embedding is a lookup table of parameters

`nn.Embedding(n, k)` is an $n \times k$ table of trainable numbers. Indexing
it with a tensor of integers returns the matching rows. A person embedding of
width 1 is a column of $\theta_p$; an item embedding of width 1 is a column
of $d_i$. There is no "input layer" in the usual sense: the index *is* the
input.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
import torch.nn as nn
theta = nn.Embedding(n_p, 1)        # one number per person
theta.weight.shape, theta(P[:3])    # rows for the first three training cells
```

### 3. The forward pass is the item response function

For the 2PL the logit is $a_i \theta_p + d_i$: look up three numbers and
combine them. A `Module` packages the lookups and the combination, and its
`forward` method is the item response function on the logit scale. The
sigmoid that turns a logit into a probability is folded into the loss below,
which is numerically safer than applying it here.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
class TwoPLNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_persons, n_items):
        super().__init__()
        self.theta = nn.Embedding(n_persons, 1)   # person ability
        self.a = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1)         # item slope (signed)
        self.d = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1)         # item intercept (= -a * difficulty)
        nn.init.normal_(self.theta.weight, std=0.1)
        nn.init.ones_(self.a.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.d.weight)

    def forward(self, p, i):
        return (self.a(i) * self.theta(p) + self.d(i)).squeeze(-1)

net = TwoPLNet(n_p, n_i)
logits = net(P[:5], I[:5])
logits, torch.sigmoid(logits)
```

At initialisation every item has slope 1 and intercept 0 and every person is
near 0, so every probability is about one half.

### 4. The loss is the negative log-likelihood

`BCEWithLogitsLoss` is $-\frac{1}{n}\sum_c \big[y_c \log p_c + (1-y_c)\log(1-p_c)\big]$
with $p_c = \sigma(\text{logit}_c)$: the mean negative log-likelihood of a
Bernoulli model, which is exactly the quantity an IRT package maximises.
Before training it is $\log 2 \approx 0.693$, the log-loss of a fair coin.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
loss_fn(net(P, I), Y).item()
```

### 5. A prior on persons, but not on items

Persons and items are both parameters here, but they are not in the same
position. Each item is answered by thousands of persons, so its slope and
intercept are pinned down by the data and need no help. Each person answers
a dozen to a hundred items, and there is a new $\theta_p$ for every person
added to the sample, so the person parameters never stop multiplying. Fitting
a free $\theta_p$ for every person by maximum likelihood is joint maximum
likelihood, which is inconsistent as the number of persons grows
[@haberman1977maximum] and runs away for perfect scores. IRT software avoids
this by integrating $\theta$ out under a $N(0,1)$ prior, which is marginal
maximum likelihood [@bock1981marginal]; the item parameters are left as
free fixed effects, exactly as they are here. The network's equivalent is to
add $\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_p \theta_p^2$ to the loss, scaled by $1/n$ to match
the mean log-likelihood. That makes the fit a MAP estimate under the same
normal prior, and it is a single line. Nothing here puts a prior on the item
slopes, and the networks do not need one for the comparison.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def objective(net, p, i, y, n=len(train)):
    nll = loss_fn(net(p, i), y)
    prior = 0.5 * (net.theta(p) ** 2).sum() / n          # N(0,1) prior on theta
    return nll + prior
```

(The helper module spreads the prior over each person's responses so that it
is unbiased in a minibatch; the idea is the same.)

### 6. The training loop

Gradient descent on the objective, in minibatches, with Adam as the
optimiser. Each pass over the training cells is an epoch. This is the whole
algorithm; everything else is monitoring.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
torch.manual_seed(SEED)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=0.02)
n, batch = len(train), 4096
for epoch in range(10):
    perm = torch.randperm(n)
    for s in range(0, n, batch):
        j = perm[s:s + batch]
        opt.zero_grad()
        objective(net, P[j], I[j], Y[j]).backward()
        opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        print(f"epoch {epoch + 1:2d}  train log-loss {loss_fn(net(P, I), Y).item():.4f}")
```

Ten epochs take a few seconds on a laptop CPU, and the training log-loss
settles at the value the 2PL can reach on this table. Held-out predictions
are the same forward pass on the held-out indices, through a sigmoid:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
test = d[d.test]
with torch.no_grad():
    p_test = torch.sigmoid(net(torch.tensor(test.pid.values), torch.tensor(test.iid.values))).numpy()
log_loss(test.resp.values, p_test)
```

That is a complete item response model, fit by a neural-network toolkit, in
about thirty lines. The Rasch model drops the slope. The multidimensional
model makes the embeddings wider. The MLP replaces the dot product with
hidden layers. All four live in the helper module with the same training
loop (`fit`), which also records train and held-out loss per epoch.

## The network recovers what mirt recovers

First, the Rasch and 2PL models from the helper module, trained with the
same loop as above on the residency exam, each reported by its training and
held-out log-loss after the final epoch. The 2PL's held-out loss is the
number to carry forward: everything else on the page is scored against it.

```{python}
#| label: fit-one
#| code-summary: "Fit Rasch and 2PL on the residency exam"
rasch, h_rasch = fit(Rasch(n_p, n_i), d)
twopl, h_2pl = fit(TwoPL(n_p, n_i), d)
for name, h in (("Rasch", h_rasch), ("2PL", h_2pl)):
    last = h.iloc[-1]
    print(f"{name:6s} after {int(last.epoch)} epochs: "
          f"train log-loss {last.train:.4f}, held-out log-loss {last.test:.4f}")
```

Does the network recover the item parameters? The offline `mirt` 2PL fit
wrote its slopes and intercepts next to its predictions, so we can compare
item by item.

```{python}
#| label: fig-recovery
#| code-summary: "Item parameters: PyTorch against mirt"
ref = pd.read_csv("nn_irt_data/borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt_mirt_2pl_items.csv", dtype={"item": str})
ref = ref.set_index("item").reindex(sorted(d["item"].unique()))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))
ax[0].scatter(ref.d, twopl.d.weight.detach().numpy().ravel(), s=12)
ax[0].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL intercept $d$", ylabel="PyTorch 2PL intercept $d$")
sd_theta = twopl.theta.weight.detach().numpy().std()
ax[1].scatter(ref.a, twopl.a.weight.detach().numpy().ravel() * sd_theta, s=12)
ax[1].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL slope $a$", ylabel=r"PyTorch 2PL slope $a \times \mathrm{sd}(\hat\theta)$")
for a_ in ax:
    lo, hi = a_.get_xlim(); a_.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], "k--", lw=0.8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The intercepts agree to the dot. The slopes agree once the scale of $\theta$
is accounted for: `mirt` fixes the *population* variance of $\theta$ at one,
while the network's point estimates are shrunk by the prior and have a
smaller spread, so its raw slopes are proportionally larger. Multiplying them
by the spread of $\hat\theta$ puts the two on the same footing. The
remaining scatter is the difference between a point estimate for each person
and integrating the person out, to which we return below.

# Part II. Width and depth on 24 tables {#part-ii}

## Wider networks overfit, and early stopping is the fix

Now the models that are not classical IRT, still on the residency exam.
Before looking, it helps to say what to expect. Training loss should fall
in order of parameter count: a model with more freedom can always fit the
cells it is shown at least as well as a model with less, so the Rasch curve
should sit highest, the 2PL below it, and the three wider models below
that. Held-out loss is a different matter. Extra parameters only help there
if they capture something that generalises from a person's training cells
to their held-out ones; if they do not, the model spends its freedom
memorising the training cells, and held-out loss turns upward after an
early minimum. On a test built to measure one thing, the anticipation is
therefore that the wider models will win on the left panel and lose on the
right, and that the losing will be worst for the model with the most
parameters.

```{python}
#| label: fig-curves
#| code-summary: "Training and held-out loss by epoch, five models"
curves = {}
curves["Rasch"] = h_rasch
curves["2PL"] = h_2pl
_, curves["MIRT k=2"] = fit(Bilinear(n_p, n_i, 2), d, epochs=30)
_, curves["MLP small"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(16,)), d, epochs=30)
_, curves["MLP large"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(64, 64)), d, epochs=30)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharey=False)
for name, h in curves.items():
    ax[0].plot(h.epoch, h.train, label=name)
    ax[1].plot(h.epoch, h.test, label=name)
ax[0].set(title="training log-loss", xlabel="epoch", ylabel="log-loss")
ax[1].set(title="held-out log-loss", xlabel="epoch")
ax[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

That is what happens. On the left, the Rasch and 2PL curves flatten within
ten epochs at the value each model can reach, and the three wider models
keep going, ending a full 0.01 below the 2PL in training loss. On the
right, the 2PL is the best held-out model at every epoch after the first
few. The MIRT model touches the 2PL's held-out loss around its third or
fourth epoch and then drifts slowly upward; the small multilayer perceptron
does the same with more noise; the large one is at its best around the fourth
epoch and by epoch thirty has given back about 0.006 of that, ending 0.008
behind the 2PL and only just ahead of the Rasch model, having fit the training
cells better than anything else on the page. The gap between the two panels is overfitting made visible, and it
widens with parameter count, as anticipated.

Two practical consequences follow. First, the wider models have to be
stopped early, and their best held-out epoch arrives fast, after three to
five passes over the data, so every model in the comparison below is
reported at its best held-out epoch rather than at convergence. Second, the
test length matters: a person with 93 training responses, as here, pins
their $\theta_p$ down well enough that the 2PL barely overfits at all,
which is why its held-out curve is flat. On shorter tests even the 2PL
starts to drift, and we return to that below.

### Held-out IMV across 24 tables

```{python}
#| label: fit-all
#| code-summary: "Fit all PyTorch models on all tables"
from pathlib import Path

def best_epoch_preds(model_fn, d, epochs=30):
    """Train, keep the predictions from the epoch with lowest held-out loss."""
    te = d[d.test]
    best = (np.inf, None)
    model = model_fn()
    hist = []
    for ep in range(epochs):
        model, h = fit(model, d, epochs=1, seed=SEED + ep)
        p = predict(model, te)
        ll = log_loss(te.resp.values, p)
        hist.append(ll)
        if ll < best[0]:
            best = (ll, p)
    return best[1]

nn_specs = {
    "Rasch": lambda n_p, n_i: Rasch(n_p, n_i),
    "2PL": lambda n_p, n_i: TwoPL(n_p, n_i),
    "MIRT k=2": lambda n_p, n_i: Bilinear(n_p, n_i, 2),
    "MLP small": lambda n_p, n_i: MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(16,)),
    "MLP large": lambda n_p, n_i: MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(64, 64)),
}
preds = {}
for t, d in data.items():
    n_p, n_i = d.pid.max() + 1, d.iid.max() + 1
    te = d[d.test]
    preds[t] = {"y": te.resp.values}
    for name, mk in nn_specs.items():
        preds[t][name] = best_epoch_preds(lambda: mk(n_p, n_i), d)
    mp = FITS / f"{t}_mirt_preds.csv.gz"
    if not mp.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"no mirt predictions for {t} at {mp}; run nn_irt_mirt_compute.R first")
    m = pd.read_csv(mp, dtype={"id": str, "item": str})
    m = te[["id", "item"]].merge(m, on=["id", "item"], how="left")
    for c in m.columns:
        if c.startswith("mirt_"):
            preds[t][c] = m[c].values
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-imv
#| code-summary: "IMV chart"
rows = []
for t, pr in preds.items():
    y = pr["y"]
    for name, p in pr.items():
        if name in ("y", "2PL") or np.isnan(p).all():
            continue
        rows.append({"table": t, "model": name, "log-loss": log_loss(y, p),
                     "IMV vs 2PL": vanilla_imv(pr["2PL"], p, y)})
res = pd.DataFrame(rows)
order = [m for m in ["Rasch", "MIRT k=2", "MLP small", "MLP large",
                     "mirt_2pl", "mirt_monopoly", "mirt_lpe"] if m in set(res.model)]
labels = {"mirt_2pl": "mirt 2PL", "mirt_monopoly": "mirt monotonic poly.", "mirt_lpe": "mirt LPE"}
imv_tab = res.pivot(index="table", columns="model", values="IMV vs 2PL").reindex(TABLES)[order]

# tables grouped, and within a group ordered by the MIRT gain (used by the table below)
group_colour = dict(zip(GROUPS, ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#2f9e6e", "#8e5bd6", "#c9a227"]))
rows_order = []
for g, ts in GROUPS.items():
    ts = [t for t in ts if t in imv_tab.index]
    rows_order += sorted(ts, key=lambda t: -imv_tab.loc[t, "MIRT k=2"])
imv_tab = imv_tab.reindex(rows_order)

records = [{"table": r.table, "short": SHORT[r.table], "group": GROUP_OF[r.table],
            "model": r.model, "imv": round(float(r["IMV vs 2PL"]), 4)} for _, r in res.iterrows()]
display(HTML(imv_stripchart_html(records, order, labels, group_colour)))
```

Each row is one model and each dot is one table, coloured by the kind of
instrument. Dots to the right of zero mean the model predicts held-out
responses better than the PyTorch 2PL on that table; the 2PL is the zero
line, so it has no row of its own. Hover over or tap a dot to pick out that
table in every row and see its values. Three Rasch losses beyond the edge of
the window are drawn as triangles.

One row needs reading before the others. **The `mirt 2PL` row is the same
model as the zero line, and its dots are not at zero.** They are all to the
right, from nothing to 0.03. That is the difference between two estimators
of one model, not between two models, and we take it apart below. For now,
note that it fixes which comparisons are fair: networks against the PyTorch
2PL (same estimator), and flexible item curves against the `mirt` 2PL (same
estimator).

```{python}
#| label: imv-rule
#| echo: false
# A rule between the two column blocks of the table below. The boundary is computed
# rather than hardcoded so it follows the table if the model list changes: one cell
# for the row label, then the IMV columns, so the first log-loss column is child
# imv_tab.shape[1] + 2.
cut = imv_tab.shape[1] + 2
display(HTML(
    f"<style>#tbl-imv table thead tr:first-child th:nth-child(3),"
    f"#tbl-imv table thead tr:nth-child(2) th:nth-child({cut}),"
    f"#tbl-imv table tbody tr > :nth-child({cut})"

```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-imv
#| code-summary: "The numbers: IMV vs 2PL and held-out log-loss"
ll2 = pd.Series({t: log_loss(pr["y"], pr["2PL"]) for t, pr in preds.items()}, name="2PL")
ll_tab = res.pivot(index="table", columns="model", values="log-loss").reindex(rows_order)[order]
ll_tab.insert(0, "2PL", ll2.reindex(rows_order))
out = pd.concat({"IMV vs 2PL": imv_tab.round(4), "held-out log-loss": ll_tab.round(4)}, axis=1)
out.index = [SHORT[t] for t in out.index]
# display names only: fig-gap still indexes imv_tab by the raw column names
out = out.rename(columns=labels, level=1)

out
```

## On tests built to measure one thing, nothing beats the 2PL

Across the achievement and ability tests, the knowledge tests and two of the
three exams with a documented multidimensional structure, the wider networks
sit within about 0.01 IMV of the 2PL, and as often below it as above. For
calibration, the IMV paper puts the gain from 1PL to 2PL on typical
cognitive data at roughly the value of knowing someone's age when predicting
chronic disease; the gains here are a fraction of that, and they go both
ways. The ECPE grammar test is the instructive case. It has a known
three-attribute Q-matrix, and a model built to find structure still predicts
no better, because the attributes are too correlated to carry separate
signal in held-out cells. Structure that is real in the design can be
invisible in prediction. The one clear exception in this group is the FSIQ
mental-rotation test, where every wider network gains about 0.03. We first read
that as the test failing to be unidimensional in practice whatever it was built
to measure. The sweep below says otherwise: 42% of its items take a negative
2PL slope, the highest share of any table named on this page, and the second
dimension lines up with that split almost perfectly. The gain is scoring, not
spatial ability.

## Where the networks win, a two-dimensional 2PL wins too

The gains cluster in the personality and clinical inventories: about 0.03 on
the ADQ anhedonia scale, 0.02 on the Eysenck EPI (three scales in one
table), 0.008 on the Woodworth, with smaller gains on the Author Recognition
Test and the GMI. Seven of the 24 tables show a gain above 0.005 and the
other seventeen sit within noise of the 2PL, so the positive result rests on a
minority of these tables; that is what one would expect if a second dimension is
something an instrument has or lacks rather than a general property of item
response data. In every one of these the MLPs match or trail the
two-dimensional MIRT, and the large MLP is never reliably better than the
small one. Once the embeddings are two-dimensional, a nonlinear decoder adds
nothing on these data. Put differently: the signal a network can find in a
person-by-item table of this kind is a second dimension, and an ordinary
two-dimensional 2PL finds it. Depth is not where the signal is. What that second dimension
*is* turns out to vary, and the close of [Part III](#part-iii) takes that
question up.

The Rasch row shows the same thing from the other side. Its large losses
(0.11 on the NPI, 0.08 on the ADQ, 0.07 on the Denver screener) are tables
where slopes differ sharply across items, including reverse-keyed items a
Rasch model cannot fit at all. The step from one item parameter to two is
worth more than every step after it.

## Flexible item curves do not add much

The asymmetric LPE curve tracks the `mirt` 2PL to within 0.003 on every table,
very slightly above it on average. The monotonic polynomial is the same on the
tests and worse on several inventories (0.04 below on the NPI, 0.015 on the
ADQ), and it failed to converge on three of the longer tables. Changing the
shape of the item curve while keeping one dimension buys a little on some tables
and loses more on others. The [asymmetric IRT vignette](asymmetric_irt.qmd)
reaches the same verdict from a different direction, taking the three asymmetric
models of @shimbonifay2026 across dozens of binary IRW tables with the same IMV:
the plain 2PL wins outright on the largest share, and the best case in that
batch is worth about what a typical 1PL-to-2PL upgrade is worth. On dichotomous
tables the 2PL's logistic curve is good enough, and the only thing worth adding
is a dimension, when the instrument has one to add.

## The mirt 2PL gap is an estimator effect, and it is largest on short tests

The same 2PL fit by marginal maximum likelihood beats the gradient-descent
fit by 0.03 on the 25-item COVID knowledge test, by 0.009 on the 30-item
ENCCEJA form and the 18-item financial literacy test, and by nothing on the
116-item residency exam. The Denver screener, with 105 items, looks like an
exception until one remembers it is age-adaptive: each child answers only
the items near their age, about thirty in training, so it is a short test in
the sense that matters. Plotting the gap against the number of training
responses each person contributes makes the pattern plain.

```{python}
#| label: fig-gap
#| code-summary: "Estimator gap against test length"
gap = imv_tab["mirt_2pl"]
n_resp = pd.Series({t: float(data[t][~data[t].test].groupby("pid").size().median()) for t in gap.index})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.scatter(n_resp, gap, s=28, color=[group_colour[GROUP_OF[t]] for t in gap.index])
for t in gap.index:
    if gap[t] > 0.008:
        ax.annotate(SHORT[t], (n_resp[t], gap[t]), fontsize=7, xytext=(4, 2), textcoords="offset points")
ax.axhline(0, color="0.3", lw=0.8)
ax.set(xlabel="median training responses per person", ylabel="IMV of mirt 2PL over PyTorch 2PL")
ax.grid(color="0.9", lw=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for sp in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Why does it happen? The networks here treat each person's $\theta$ as a
parameter to be estimated, and the item parameters are then fit around those
point estimates. With a dozen or twenty responses per person those estimates
are poor, and the item parameters inherit the error, which is the
incidental-parameter problem; `mirt` integrates the persons out instead. That
is a story about the estimator rather than the model, and it is worth more than
a paragraph, so [Part IV](#part-iv) takes it apart. We have left the network as
it is so that the effect stays visible here: it is the price of the simplest
possible estimator, and readers who build their own networks should know it is
there.

# Part III. How often does width pay? {#part-iii}

## Away from the hand-picked tables, the median table gains nothing


Twenty-four tables chosen to span kinds of structure cannot tell us how often
a second dimension pays. For that we need a rule rather than a judgment, so we
applied one to the whole warehouse: dichotomous, at least 500 respondents, at
least 10 items, and density at least 0.9, which is what the cell-level split
needs. That gives 262 tables, of which 242 fit without incident. The sweep is
narrower than Part II's comparison — it is the 2PL against a two-dimensional
MIRT and nothing else, because the point is to count how often the one move
that worked above actually works, not to re-run five models 242 times.

```{python}
#| label: fig-expand
#| code-summary: "The sweep: 242 tables under a selection rule"
ex = pd.read_csv(DATA / "expand_summary.csv")
picked = ex.table.isin(TABLES)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
bins = np.linspace(-0.025, 0.105, 53)
ax.hist(ex.imv, bins=bins, color="0.78", edgecolor="white", lw=0.5, label=f"all {len(ex)} tables")
ax.hist(ex.imv[picked], bins=bins, color="#2a78d6", edgecolor="white", lw=0.5,
        label=f"{int(picked.sum())} of the 24 hand-picked")
ax.axvline(0, color="0.3", lw=0.8)
ax.axvline(ex.imv.mean(), color="#eb6834", lw=1.2, ls="--",
           label=f"mean {ex.imv.mean():+.4f}")
ax.set(xlabel="IMV of MIRT k=2 over the 2PL, held-out cells", ylabel="tables", yscale="log")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax.grid(color="0.9", lw=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for sp in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

q = ex.imv.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
print(f"mean {ex.imv.mean():+.4f}   median {q[0.5]:+.4f}   sd {ex.imv.std():.4f}")
print(f"quartiles {q[0.25]:+.4f} / {q[0.75]:+.4f}   max {ex.imv.max():+.4f}   min {ex.imv.min():+.4f}")
print(f"at or below zero: {(ex.imv <= 0).mean():.0%}    above 0.005: {(ex.imv > 0.005).mean():.0%}")
print(f"The 24 hand-picked tables, scored the same way: n={int(picked.sum())}, "
      f"mean {ex.imv[picked].mean():+.4f}, above 0.005: {(ex.imv[picked] > 0.005).mean():.0%}")
```

Note the log scale on the count axis: without it the spike at zero flattens
everything else. The median table gains **nothing at all** (−0.0001), 54% of
tables are at or below zero, and the quartiles are −0.0012 and +0.0016. The
mean is +0.0025, and it is positive only because of a thin right tail: 14% of
tables gain more than 0.005 and a single table gains 0.10. So the honest
summary of the one move that worked in Part II is that it works on about a
seventh of the warehouse and does nothing on the rest.

Two checks are worth pausing on. The first is that this mean is almost exactly
the published one. @domingue2024imv fit an exploratory two-factor model to 60
IRW datasets under a similar rule and report a mean IMV of +0.0031 against the
2PL, with a maximum of 0.029; we get +0.0025 from a different implementation,
a different split design and four times as many tables. Two independent routes
to the same number is about as much reassurance as this kind of comparison
affords.

The second is less comfortable. Scored under the same rule and the same split, the 24
give a mean of +0.0048 with 27% above 0.005 — roughly double the corpus
rate on both counts. **The hand-picked set is
enriched for the effect it reports.** That is what picking tables to span kinds
of structure does, and it was the right choice for showing *where* the gains
come from, but it makes the 24 useless for saying *how common* they are. Of the
24, 22 clear the rule; the two that do not are the developmental screeners,
which are age-adaptive and so fail the density threshold.

## The tables that gain are the ones with items running both ways

Fourteen per cent of tables gain more than 0.005, and they are not a random
fourteen per cent. IRW does not harmonise the direction of responses, and the
2PL fits an item that runs against the rest of its test by giving it a negative
slope. Counting those slopes sorts the sweep more sharply than anything else we
tried, and it sorts it as a step rather than a gradient. The 155 tables with no
negatively-sloped item gain nothing (mean $-0.0004$), and neither do the 45
where under a tenth of the slopes are negative (mean $+0.0003$, with 3 of 45
clearing 0.005). The whole of the sweep's average gain comes from the remaining
42, where more than a tenth do: mean $+0.0158$, median $+0.0033$, and 19 of 42
above 0.005.

Why those items oppose the rest is a separate question, and not one held-out
prediction can answer. Some are reverse-worded items that were never recoded,
some are bipolar by design, one is a test whose respondents differ in age
cohort, and in the option-level tables a negative slope is simply a distractor.
We never read a line of item wording. The statistics, the instruments and the
checks that would settle it are set out in
[issue #3197](https://github.com/ben-domingue/irw/issues/3197); they do not
belong on this page.

The consequence for [Part II](#part-ii) is a qualification rather than a
reversal. That a two-dimensional 2PL finds whatever a deeper network finds is a
claim about depth, and nothing in the sweep touches it. What changes is the
reading of the gains: a reader tempted to take a high IMV as evidence of a
second trait should check the sign of the slopes first.

# Part IV. Which estimator closes the gap to mirt? {#part-iv}

[Part II](#part-ii) left a promise unkept: the same 2PL, fit in torch and in
`mirt`, does not give the same held-out loss, and the gap is largest on short
tests. This part takes it apart. It is an aside rather than part of the main
argument, which is why it is short, but anyone who builds the networks above
will meet the same gap --- and one of our attempts to close it was wrong in an
instructive way.

Two things differ between the torch 2PL and the `mirt` 2PL. One is how the scale
of the person parameters is set: the PyTorch 2PL puts an $N(0,1)$ penalty on
$\theta$, while `mirt` fixes its population variance by assumption. The other is
the estimator: the PyTorch model is fit by gradient descent on the joint
likelihood, with each person's $\theta$ treated as a parameter, while `mirt`
integrates the persons out. We fit the same 2PL six ways on the same training
cells, scored on the same held-out cells, to separate the two.

The six are: **Adam with the prior**, the network used throughout the page;
**Adam constrained**, with $\theta$ standardised in the forward pass and no
penalty; **alternating JML**, Newton block updates of persons and items in turn,
in both a prior and a constrained version; **EM marginal maximum likelihood**,
the estimator `mirt` uses, with a posterior over a quadrature grid; and **MML by
L-BFGS**, the same marginal likelihood maximised directly with autograd. The
joint and alternating estimators predict with point estimates of $\theta$; EM and
MML predict with the posterior.

One thing to note before the table: the penalty fixes the scale only weakly. In
the likelihood $a_i\theta_p$ is all that matters, so the same fit can be written
with a small $\theta$ and a large $a$, and the penalty pulls $\theta$ toward zero
at a constant price. Run alternating JML without early stopping on the residency
exam and over 2,000 sweeps the person SD falls from 0.55 to 0.04 while the median
slope rises from 1.1 to 13 --- with the held-out log-loss unmoved at 0.5482
throughout, because $a\theta$ is what the likelihood sees. The constrained
version fixes the scale exactly, and that is the only difference between the two
alternating fits.

```{python}
#| label: fig-estimators
#| code-summary: "Each estimator against the PyTorch 2PL, all 24 tables"
est_rows, nresp = [], {}
for t in TABLES:
    d = prepare(t)
    te = d[d.test]
    m = te[["id", "item"]].merge(pd.read_csv(FITS / f"{t}_mirt_preds.csv.gz", dtype={"id": str, "item": str}),
                                 on=["id", "item"], how="left")
    e = pd.read_csv(FITS / f"{t}_estimation_preds.csv.gz")
    tp = pd.read_csv(FITS / f"{t}_torch_preds.csv.gz")
    y = e.y.values
    base = tp["2PL"].values            # the page's zero line throughout: Adam, prior
    cand = {"mirt 2PL": m["mirt_2pl"].values,
            "L-BFGS (MML)": e["MML L-BFGS"].values,
            "EM (MML)": e["EM MML"].values,
            "Adam, constrained": tp["2PL (constr.)"].values,
            "alt. JML, prior": e["alt JML (prior)"].values,
            "alt. JML, constrained": e["alt JML (constr.)"].values}
    for k, pr in cand.items():
        est_rows.append({"table": t, "short": SHORT[t], "group": GROUP_OF[t],
                         "model": k, "imv": round(float(vanilla_imv(base, pr, y)), 4)})
    nresp[SHORT[t]] = float(d[~d.test].groupby("pid").size().median())
nresp = pd.Series(nresp)
est = pd.DataFrame(est_rows)
est_order = ["mirt 2PL", "L-BFGS (MML)", "EM (MML)",
             "Adam, constrained", "alt. JML, prior", "alt. JML, constrained"]
display(HTML(imv_stripchart_html(est.to_dict("records"), est_order, {}, group_colour,
                                 div_id="est-strip", xlim=0.03,
                                 xlabel="IMV relative to the PyTorch 2PL (Adam, prior)")))

wide = est.pivot(index="table", columns="model", values="imv")[est_order]
print(wide.mean().round(4).rename("mean over tables").to_string())
print(f"\nlargest gap to mirt over the 24 tables: L-BFGS {(wide['L-BFGS (MML)'] - wide['mirt 2PL']).abs().max():.4f}, "
      f"EM {(wide['EM (MML)'] - wide['mirt 2PL']).abs().max():.4f}")
```

The zero line is the PyTorch 2PL fit by Adam with the prior --- the model used
everywhere else on this page --- so it has no row of its own, and a dot to the
right means that estimator predicts the held-out cells better than it does.
This is the same baseline, the same colours and the same gesture as
@fig-imv: hover or tap a dot to pick out that table in every row. Three
things stand out.

**The torch MML matches mirt.** The top three rows are one model fit by three
marginal-likelihood routines --- `mirt`'s own, our EM, and our L-BFGS --- and
they lie on top of each other at about +0.005. The L-BFGS row never differs
from the `mirt` row by more than 0.003 on any table and the EM row by more than
0.03, and the handful of tables carrying those differences are the ASQ and
Denver screeners and EDSC, where several items are nearly perfectly separated
by the persons, their parameters sit at magnitudes in the hundreds and the
likelihood is flat along them. On the two screeners the torch fit has the
higher marginal likelihood of the pair. Same model, same objective, same
predictions --- which is what makes the rows below the comparison worth
reading.

**The gap is the estimator.** The figure splits cleanly in half. Every
estimator that integrates the persons out sits above zero, by about +0.005;
every estimator that plugs in a point estimate of $\theta$ sits at zero or
below. Nothing else lines up with that split --- not the optimiser, since EM
and L-BFGS converge and agree with each other, and not the treatment of the
scale, since the prior and constrained versions fall on the same side. What
differs is whether the person parameters are integrated out or treated as
known. The +0.005 is also the `mirt 2PL` row of @fig-imv, which is where this
question came from; it is the same number, and this is its explanation.

**Alternation does not help.** Alternating joint maximum likelihood is the
textbook way to fit a joint model, and it is worse than Adam, by 0.003 for the
prior version and by 0.012 for the constrained one. The incidental-parameter
problem predicts exactly this. The best held-out
sweep falls within the first ten on 22 of 24 tables for the prior version and on
all 24 for the constrained one (medians three and two), and the constrained fit
stopped on patience rather than convergence on 18 tables. On short tests the loss
then rises: on the COVID knowledge test it goes from 0.690 at sweep one to 0.81
by sweep ten and 0.98 for the constrained version by sweep twenty, as some items
separate the persons and their slopes run away. The constrained fit is worst on
the Onah test, 20 training responses per person, where the gap to `mirt` is 0.185.

## Constraining the scale does not close it, and it costs a little

Fixing $\theta$ at $N(0,1)$ exactly removes the drift above. On the residency exam
it recovers `mirt`'s item parameters about as well as the prior version does:
intercepts agree closely in both, and slopes agree once the scale is handled, the
constrained ones about 9% above `mirt`'s and the rescaled prior ones about 3%
above. What it does not do is close the prediction gap.

```{python}
#| label: fig-constrained
#| code-summary: "What fixing the scale costs, by test length"
models = ["Rasch", "2PL", "MIRT k=2", "MLP small", "MLP large"]
con_rows = []
for t in TABLES:
    d = prepare(t)
    y = d[d.test].resp.values
    tp = pd.read_csv(FITS / f"{t}_torch_preds.csv.gz")
    base = tp["2PL"].values
    for name in models:
        # baseline is the SAME network fit with the prior, so no third model
        # enters: a dot is what fixing the scale buys or costs that network.
        cost = vanilla_imv(tp[name].values, tp[f"{name} (constr.)"].values, y)
        con_rows.append({"table": t, "short": SHORT[t], "group": GROUP_OF[t], "panel": name,
                         "x": int(nresp[SHORT[t]]), "y": round(float(cost), 4)})
con = pd.DataFrame(con_rows)
notes = {m: f"mean {con[con.panel == m].y.mean():+.4f}" for m in models}
display(HTML(facet_scatter_html(con.to_dict("records"), models, group_colour,
                                div_id="con-facets", notes=notes,
                                xlabel="median training responses per person",
                                ylabel="IMV over the same network fit with the prior")))

# how strongly the cost depends on test length, per panel -- quoted in the text
# below, so computed here rather than typed in
w = con.pivot(index="short", columns="panel", values="y")[models]
ln = np.log(con.groupby("short").x.first()[w.index])
print("corr(log median responses per person, cost):")
print("  " + "   ".join(f"{m} {np.corrcoef(ln, w[m])[0, 1]:+.2f}" for m in models))
```

The baseline here is not the 2PL. Each panel scores one network's constrained
fit against **the same network fit with the prior**, so a dot at zero means
fixing the scale changed nothing for that model on that table, and a dot below
zero means it cost something. Nothing is compared across panels, which is why
the Rasch panel can sit at zero while the MLP panels sit below it without that
being a statement about Rasch versus an MLP.

The Rasch panel is worth pausing on, because it first told us something false. With
the Rasch model written the usual way --- $\theta_p + d_i$, no slope --- the
constraint was catastrophic: worse on every one of the 24 tables, by 0.03 on
average and by 0.19 on the Onah test. That is not what it costs to fix the scale.
It is what it costs to fix the scale with nothing left to absorb it. The prior
version lets the data set the spread of $\theta$, which comes out at 0.56 on the
residency exam and 0.40 on the Onah test, and a slopeless Rasch has no way to
express that the spread should not be one. Giving it a single slope $c$ shared by
every item --- still a Rasch model, since the items continue to differ only in
difficulty --- removes the problem entirely: the constrained Rasch is then within
0.0001 of the prior version on average and ahead of it on half the tables. The
lesson is about identification, not about the constraint: a model that cannot
represent the scale should not be asked to fix it.

With that repaired, the cost of the constraint is small and consistent across
the five networks: the panel means run from zero for the Rasch model to
$-0.003$ for the large MLP. In four of the five panels it is also concentrated
where theory says it should be. The Rasch model, the 2PL, the MIRT and the small
MLP all fan out below zero at the left, where people answer few items, and close
toward the zero line at the right; the correlations printed under the figure run
from +0.30 to +0.45 for those four, and the spread of the costs halves or better
between the short tables and the long ones. The large MLP is the exception and
worth noting as one: it pays about $-0.003$ whatever the test length, and its
correlation is the +0.05 at the end of that printed line. Whatever it is losing
to the constraint is not the thing short tests cause. Standardising $\theta$ divides out the spread of estimates
that are mostly noise on a short test, stretching poorly determined person
parameters back to a spread of one instead of shrinking them toward zero. That is
the incidental-parameter story again, seen from the other side. The constraint
also does nothing to stop the wide networks overfitting: they reach their best
held-out loss early and climb after it in both versions. Early stopping is still
what keeps them honest.

# Limitations

## Of the model comparison

- **The held-out set is also the validation set.** Each PyTorch model is
  reported at its best held-out epoch, which flatters every network by a
  small amount and the wider ones by slightly more, since they have more
  epochs at which to get lucky. A third split would fix this; we judged that
  at 24 tables and five models the bias is small relative to the effects
  reported, and the direction is known: it works against the 2PL, not for
  it. Note that the same practice tilts Part IV the other way. There the
  networks and the alternating JML fits stop on the held-out cells while
  `mirt` never sees them, so the estimator gap reported there is if anything
  an underestimate. In both parts the thumb is on the networks' side.
- **Two estimators, one model.** The PyTorch 2PL (MAP by gradient descent)
  and the `mirt` 2PL (marginal maximum likelihood) are the same model and do
  not give the same held-out loss. The comparison that is fair is therefore
  networks against the PyTorch 2PL and flexible curves against the `mirt`
  2PL, and Parts I to III are written that way. Part IV shows that an
  estimator which integrates over the persons closes the gap in torch, and that
  fixing the scale of $\theta$ does not.
- **Only person and item identities enter the model.** The networks see
  exactly what the classical models see, so this is a comparison of
  functional forms, not of information. Sequential models of learning
  [@piech2015dkt] use the order of responses; models with item text as input
  can predict items never seen in training; variational IRT replaces the
  point estimates with an encoder network. All of these use more than the
  (person, item, response) triple, and all can be scored with the same
  held-out cells and the same IMV, but none is on this page.
- **Dichotomous, dense tables only.** The cell-level split and the
  Bernoulli loss are written for 0/1 responses. Polytomous tables need a
  different output layer and a different loss; sparse tables raise the
  question of whether the missingness is informative.
- **Subsampling.** Tables are capped at 5,000 respondents and 116 items.
  The gains reported for the inventories are therefore gains at that size;
  a wider network may do relatively better with more data, which is the
  usual pattern and is not tested here.
- **Twenty-four tables, chosen by hand.** The groups were picked to span
  kinds of structure, not sampled from the warehouse, and the counts per
  group are small. The qualitative pattern (dimension helps where there is
  one, depth does not) is consistent across the groups; the sizes of the
  gains are specific to these tables, and the sweep confirms that the set is
  enriched — roughly double the corpus rate of gains above 0.005.
- **The sweep is narrower than the comparison it generalises.** The 242-table
  sweep fits the 2PL against a two-dimensional MIRT and nothing else. It can
  say how often the one move that worked in Part II pays, and it can say what
  the paying tables have in common, but it says nothing about depth, about
  flexible item curves, or about the estimator gap — all of which rest on the
  24 tables alone. Its selection rule also caps fetched tables at two million
  responses, which excludes the largest mass administrations (the
  million-respondent ENEM forms among them), and its density threshold of 0.9
  excludes adaptive instruments, including two of the 24 hand-picked tables.
- **The sweep treats tables as independent, and the warehouse does not.** IRW
  holds several tables from some deposits, and two of them sit among the
  largest gains in the sweep (`vogel_2024_citizen_attributes_s2` and `_s3`, at
  +0.094 and +0.091). Nothing in the selection rule or the summaries accounts
  for that, so the tail is less varied than a count of 242 suggests, and any
  standard error computed as though those tables were independent would be too
  small. We report no such standard error for that reason.
- **A negative slope is a symptom, and we never read the items.** The split at
  the close of [Part III](#part-iii) counts items whose fitted 2PL slope is
  negative. That is not an observation of the wording: a slope goes negative
  for an item that was reverse-worded and never recoded, but also for a
  mis-scored key, a badly behaved item, a distractor in an option-level table,
  or an item that genuinely measures something else. We make no claim about
  which, and the sorting in Part III does not depend on one. What would settle
  it --- the instruments, the item text and the checks --- is in
  `ben-domingue/irw` issue #3197.

## Of the estimator comparison

- **Two estimators are on a common footing; the networks are not.** The MML fits
  are the same model as `mirt` and are compared directly. The Adam networks and
  the alternating JML fits are different estimators of the same model, and their
  gaps to `mirt` are gaps in estimation, not in the model.
- **Stopping uses the held-out set.** The Adam networks and both alternating JML
  fits pick their stopping point on the held-out cells, which flatters them
  slightly. The MML fits do not use held-out data at all: they maximise the training
  likelihood (EM, then four L-BFGS rounds).
- **Items with extreme parameters.** On the ASQ, Denver and EDSC screeners several
  items have parameters in the hundreds, and the marginal likelihood is flat along
  them. Two correct maximisers can stop at different points there, which is why
  the largest MML disagreements with `mirt` are on those tables.
- **Dichotomous 2PL only.** The estimators here are for the 2PL on 0/1 responses,
  and the multidimensional and nonlinear networks are not refit with them.


# Reproducibility

**Source code for this page:**
[`nn_irt.qmd`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt.qmd),
[`nn_irt_helpers.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_helpers.py),
[`nn_irt_chart.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_chart.py),
[`nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R),
and, for Part IV,
[`nn_irt_estimation.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation.py),
[`nn_irt_estimation_compute.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_compute.py)
and [`nn_irt_estimation_drift.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_drift.py).

<!-- Python-only page on Quarto's jupyter engine: the R includes used by the
     other vignettes would flip it to knitr, so the source links and version
     line are written by hand (see irt_python.qmd). -->

Results were computed on 15 October 2026 (Parts I–II) and 16 October 2026
(Part IV); the 242-table sweep on 22 October 2026. The tables were fetched on 15 October from `item_response_warehouse`
v72.0 and `item_response_warehouse_6` v5.11.

This page is rendered with Quarto's `freeze` option: the PyTorch training runs
on a laptop and the outputs are committed under `_freeze/`, so the site build
needs neither PyTorch nor a Redivis credential. The heavy intermediates behind
those outputs — the fetched tables, the splits, and the held-out predictions
from every model — are regenerable, so they are kept out of the repository in
`vignettes/nn_irt_data/fits/`, which `.gitignore` excludes. What is committed
beside the page is the small, slow-to-rebuild material: the `mirt` item
parameters, the estimator diagnostics, the drift trace, the bibliography, and
`expand_summary.csv`, the one-row-per-table result of the 242-table sweep,
which takes hours to rebuild and 26 KB to store.
Re-rendering the page from source therefore means regenerating the caches,
which needs Redivis access and an R installation; building the site from the
committed freeze needs neither. To regenerate:

```bash
# 1. A Python environment with CPU torch (from the project root)
python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
pip install irw imvpy scipy matplotlib pandas jupyter

# 2. The network fits, both versions, all tables
python vignettes/nn_irt_torch_compute.py

# 3. The 2PL three further ways on all tables, plus the drift trace (Part IV)
python vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_compute.py
python vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_drift.py

# 4. The offline mirt fits (2PL, monotonic polynomial, LPE) on the same split;
#    delete vignettes/nn_irt_data/fits/*_mirt_preds.csv.gz first if the split changes
Rscript vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R

# 5. The 242-table sweep behind the corpus check (slow: hours, and it fetches
#    most of the warehouse). Each step is resumable and skips finished tables.
#    IRW_METADATA must point at src/metadata/metadata.csv in the main checkout.
python vignettes/nn_irt_expand_compute.py    # fits/expand_results.csv
python vignettes/nn_irt_expand_loadings.py   # fits/expand_loadings.csv
python vignettes/nn_irt_expand_keying.py     # nn_irt_data/expand_summary.csv

# 6. Re-render this page
quarto render vignettes/nn_irt.qmd
```
